strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring degrees of human involvement in assisted writing beyond binary AI-text detection. The proposed likelihood-based score is simple and requires no separately trained detector.

The experiments have substantial breadth: four domains, 2,000 source documents per domain, repeated generations, multiple generators and surrogate models, and WildChat examples. The results support an association between the score and coarse levels of supplied information.

The human evaluation provides useful supporting evidence on the selected comparison set: 1,500 pairs, three independent annotators, 91.47% unanimous agreement, and 95.93% agreement between majority judgments and the input-aware metric.

The appendix documents data sources, prompts, model versions, annotation procedures, and threshold selection. The limitations appropriately distinguish informational contribution from creativity, effort, and legal authorship.
weaknesses: The central interpretation as a proportion of attributable information is insufficiently justified. Equation 5 computes a pointwise log-likelihood ratio, not Shannon mutual information; no joint prompt–output distribution establishes that the unconditional model likelihood is the relevant marginal. Even with consistent probabilities, this quantity can be negative: p(y)=0.5 and p(y|x)=0.25 produce a contribution score of -1. The Venn-diagram decomposition and percentage interpretation therefore require additional justification beyond demonstrating ordinal correlations.

The output-only derivation establishes a bound conditional on the chosen plausibility criterion, rather than establishing the minimum necessary human contribution. Equations 9–10 replace an inequality with an estimated minimum without demonstrating tightness or the existence of a prompt approaching that bound. Moreover, the mean-plus-one-standard-deviation threshold in Appendix A.5 is not a guaranteed upper bound on conditional surprisal for genuine generations. Coverage, tightness, and threshold sensitivity should be evaluated explicitly.

For a fixed model and threshold, Equation 10 is exactly a monotonic transformation of perplexity: writing h=-log p(y)/N and c=-log tau gives score=1-c/h. Consequently, its rankings and detection AUCs are identical to those obtained from perplexity. The reported detection results do not independently validate the claimed contribution interpretation, and the paper does not establish that its rescaling yields meaningful contribution percentages.

The evaluation does not adequately separate contribution measurement from easier correlates. Human-annotation pairs are selected only when the proposed input-aware metric differs by more than 0.1, so the reported agreement excludes its ambiguous comparisons and cannot establish performance on unfiltered cases. The synthetic hierarchy also varies input length and lexical overlap alongside presumed contribution. Unfiltered, stratified evaluation and comparisons against length-ratio, overlap, and likelihood baselines are needed to establish the metric's additional value.

Exact reproducibility remains uncertain despite the useful appendix. No code or constructed-data release is identified, and important likelihood-computation choices are unspecified, including chat formatting, the unconditional scoring context, special-token handling, and whether scoring probabilities incorporate generation temperature. These choices directly affect both the ratio and the calibrated threshold. Together with the unresolved attribution and minimum-contribution claims, these are important revisions needed before a positive Findings recommendation.
